claims.text: Historical parameter recommendations are not current configuration: the June recommendation and the later July recommendation use different SOL imbalance thresholds. Read the custody state for each simulated trade. (medium confidence)

The July historical analysis refers to a ten-minute imbalance window, while Jupiter’s later fee documentation says roughly the last minute. Treat the window as a version-dependent assumption that needs onchain validation. (low confidence)

A trade that reduces recent imbalance incurs no additive fee, even if imbalance remains above threshold. A worsening or sign-flipping trade can incur it above threshold; liquidations contribute to the flow state but never pay the additive fee themselves. Entry and exit therefore need separate fee calculations. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Gauntlet and Chaos Labs both reported trade splitting under the earlier size-only mechanism. The additive model was designed to address that weakness; those observations do not demonstrate current five-minute trader profitability. (medium confidence)

For a reproducible feasibility test, save contemporaneous custody parameters and the recent flow state. The documented fields include pricing.tradeImpactFeeScalar, priceImpactBuffer.deltaImbalanceThresholdDecimal, jumpRateState, increasePositionBps and decreasePositionBps. Thresholds, rounding and borrow-rate state must be replayed for each side; this is a research-method recommendation, not a claim that a historical state archive is available. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

The negation evidence scopes the claim that high volume necessarily causes high impact fees: Chaos Labs’ 2024 review says offsetting buy/sell trades can keep delta imbalance small, while informed traders trading before alpha decays can face costs that splitting does not avoid. Its historical simulations and proposed parameters should not be presented as present-day measured execution costs. (low confidence)

JLP-market cost modeling must include base fees and linear plus additive price impact on both entry and exit. Jupiter documents a 0.06% base fee per side; these rules are distinct from Beta markets, which use maker/taker fees and hourly funding. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Chaos Labs designed the additive mechanism to resist order splitting and warned that even a small trade can incur higher fees in a highly imbalanced window. Jupiter documents that all trades, including the trader’s own and liquidations, enter recent flow; splitting within the same minute does not avoid the fee. Small order size alone therefore cannot establish low-cost feasibility. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

The documented linear impact rate rounds upward to whole basis points, with a 0.01% minimum, in addition to a 0.06% base fee when opening or closing a position. A small position is therefore not exempt from per-side trading costs; borrow, swaps and network charges remain separate. A round-trip or collateral-percentage calculation must state its entry and exit notionals and leverage assumptions; it is a calculation rather than a measured trading result. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

The additive-fee state is recent net long-minus-short trade flow over roughly a minute, not total open-interest imbalance. Long opens and short closes increase it; short opens and long closes decrease it. The model should reconstruct this state at each execution rather than use a five-minute candle or aggregate open interest as its substitute. The reconstruction requirement is an inference from the documented mechanism. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Jupiter documents a 0.50% cap on base plus linear plus additive trading fees per side, rather than on every fee a trader can pay. Borrow, conditional collateral swaps and transaction charges are separate costs; treating 0.50% as an all-in round-trip ceiling would understate costs. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Collateral swaps are conditional costs: an input token differing from underlying collateral or an exit payout in another token can require a swap. Jupiter documents pool-weight adjustments to swap fees and use of the maximum input/output asset fee. Model these cash flows separately from notional trading fees instead of automatically adding the same swap percentage to every trade. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

For JLP SOL, the documented base charge applies on both opening and closing, and the linear impact rate rounds upward. A base-fee-only backtest understates even small-trade costs. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Borrow accrues continuously on full notional. A short holding period reduces accrual but does not remove it; conditional swaps and network costs also belong in the feasibility hurdle. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Feasibility inference: replay fee state at execution and model exit costs separately. Jupiter documents keeper fulfillment and a separate single-transaction path, so submission time alone does not establish a live position. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

In its July historical analysis, Chaos Labs reported lower SOL volume after the June fee update and explicitly warned that other factors could explain the association. This scopes claims that dynamic fees leave trading activity unaffected. (low confidence)

OpenJUP describes matching decoded entry events to preceding pool snapshots and later closes. This is a useful independent data-collection lead, but this pass recovered no populated trade rows and makes no performance claim from it. (low confidence)

The older Chaos Labs proposal says a close pays only the base rate, whereas Jupiter’s later documentation applies linear impact on closing. These are attributed descriptions of different dated models, not interchangeable execution rules. (low confidence)

Borrow fees accrue continuously on full position size without compounding, with utilization-dependent rates. For a constant hourly rate, a five-minute hold costs one twelfth of that hourly rate times notional; if utilization changes, integrate the changing rate. This is a cost-model implication of the documented accrual rule, not an observed five-minute rate. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Gauntlet’s September 2024 analysis optimized impact scalars and also explored joint base-fee/scalar optimization against order-book conditions. It is historical calibration evidence, not proof of current custody settings or a profitable five-minute strategy. Its conclusion explicitly recommends collecting performance data before revisiting the joint optimization. (low confidence)
